Notes: Written in March 1862 but first heard only in 1888, after Dvořák had cut it heavily, and not published until 1948; the number Op. 2 was also printed on a set of songs (B. 124) published in 1882.
Dvořák believed he had destroyed it, but copied parts turned up among Antonín Bennewitz's papers in the early 20th century; first played privately in 1932 and in public only in 2021.
At over an hour his longest chamber work; it survived only in copied parts after Dvořák destroyed the score, and was first performed in 1969.
One continuous movement in three sections, surviving only in Dvořák's own copied parts; its Andante religioso became the Nocturne in B major, Op. 40, and it was first performed in public in 1990.

Rejected by the players it was written for and never published in Dvořák's lifetime, it appeared in 1929 in a revision by Günter Raphael; its slow movement became the Romance, Op. 11, and Op. 9 was also used for two songs published in 1880.

Dvořák abandoned his revision of this originally continuous work into four movements, so the version played today was completed by Jarmil Burghauser and first performed in 1990; Op. 12 was also used for the piano Dumka and Furiant published in 1885.
His first chamber work to be published (Starý, Prague, 1875), but those parts were printed as Op. 26, the number now belonging to his Piano Trio No. 2.
Written in 1810 or 1811, it begins in g minor and ends in B-flat major, the only survivor of three early quartets in "changing, undefined keys" (D 19 and D 19A are lost).
Composed September–October 1812, its autograph was scattered, so the 1890 complete edition printed only two movements until Maurice J. E. Brown found the rest in Lund.
Dated 19 November 1812 to 21 February 1813; the minuet was written on separate leaves and added later.
Only the two outer movements survive (June–August 1813); the middle movements are presumed lost.
Once dated 1814, which explains its D number, it is now placed in 1811 or 1812, making it one of his earliest quartets.
Composed 5–13 September 1814 and first published by Spina in 1863.
Written in a week, 25 March to 1 April 1815.
Despite its number it dates from November 1813, and all four movements are in E-flat major.
Published by Josef Czerny in 1840 together with D 87 as Op. 125.

Unfinished: Grieg wrote only two movements, in Copenhagen in 1891, which Julius Röntgen edited for Peters (1908); Röntgen and later Levon Chilingirian (1999) completed movements 3 and 4 from Grieg's sketches.
